subject: Chemistry
title: Chlorophyll: Why Plants Are Green
description: A quick, practical guide to Chlorophyll: Why Plants Are Green.

hook.text: Plants are green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light for energy but reflects green light back to your eyes.

buildup.text: Chlorophyll's structure has a magnesium atom at its center, surrounded by a ring of nitrogen and carbon atoms.

discovery.text: The ring structure has alternating single and double bonds that create a system of electrons absorbing visible light.

twist.text: Green is actually wasted. Plants don't use the most abundant wavelength in sunlight—a design flaw that evolution kept.

climax.text: In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down. Hidden yellow and orange pigments emerge, and new red anthocyanins form.

punchline.text: Green is the color plants reject. Leaves are powered by red and blue light.

quiz.question: Why do leaves change color in autumn?
options: Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing hidden yellow, orange, and red pigments
Leaves absorb different light wavelengths in winter

details.summary: Chlorophyll molecules absorb red and blue wavelengths of light for photosynthesis but reflect green wavelengths, giving plants their characteristic color. The molecule's porphyrin ring with a central magnesium ion creates the specific electronic structure responsible for this absorption pattern.
details.whyItMatters: Chlorophyll's light absorption drives virtually all life on Earth by powering photosynthesis. Understanding its chemistry is essential for improving crop yields and developing artificial photosynthesis.
takeaways: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, reflecting green wavelengths
A magnesium-centered porphyrin ring creates its absorption properties
Two main types, chlorophyll a and b, absorb slightly different ranges

faq.question: Why do leaves change color in autumn if chlorophyll is always present?
faq.answer: Chlorophyll degrades as daylight hours shorten and temperatures drop. Without chlorophyll masking them, other pigments become visible: yellow and orange carotenoids were present all along, and red anthocyanins are newly produced as a protective response.

faq.question: Why do plants absorb red and blue light but not green?
faq.answer: The evolutionary reasons are debated, but chlorophyll's porphyrin ring structure happens to have energy gaps matching red and blue photon energies. Green photons have intermediate energy that does not match these gaps efficiently, so they are mostly reflected.
